title: REO Property Renovation: What to Expect in Bank-Owned Homes
metaDescription: What to expect renovating REO and bank-owned homes: winterization, freeze damage, mold, missing fixtures, code violations and servicer documentation rules.
h1: Renovating REO and Bank-Owned Properties: What to Expect
dek: REO properties are homes taken back by a lender, usually through foreclosure, and they often sit vacant for long periods. Expect winterized or freeze-damaged plumbing, moisture and mold, missing fixtures and equipment, deferred maintenance and open code violations, plus documentation requirements set by the servicer.
keyTakeaways: REO stands for real estate owned: a property a bank, servicer, GSE or other lender owns after foreclosure or a deed in lieu.
Vacancy is the root cause of most REO problems; unheated, unmonitored houses develop freeze damage, mold, pest issues and theft.
Systems often cannot be tested until utilities are restored and the house is de-winterized, so estimates carry more contingency.
Property preservation protects and maintains a vacant asset; renovation changes its condition to prepare it for sale or rent. They are different scopes with different rules.
Servicers and institutional owners require bids, photos and completion documentation in specific formats, and work outside approved scope may not be paid.

sections.body:
REO stands for real estate owned. It refers to a property that a lender or investor owns after a foreclosure sale fails to attract a third-party buyer, or after the borrower transfers the property through a deed in lieu of foreclosure. The owner may be a bank, a mortgage servicer acting for an investor, a GSE, a government agency, a fund or another mortgage lender.

REO properties sit in a particular place in the housing system. The owner did not choose to own a house; it chose to make a loan. Its goal is to resolve the asset by selling it, and sometimes by renting it, while protecting its value and meeting its obligations to investors, insurers and regulators. That goal shapes every decision about how the property is maintained and renovated.

For contractors and investors, REO work comes from two directions. Some work is done for the institutional owner, preparing the property for sale or managing its condition while it is marketed. Other work is done by the investor or homebuyer who purchases the REO, often as-is, and then renovates it.

In both cases, the physical conditions are similar. Most REO homes have been vacant for a long time, many went through a period before foreclosure when the owner could not afford maintenance, and some were damaged during or after the occupants left. A renovation plan for an REO property has to start from the assumption that the house has been unattended and that the problems you can see may not be the only ones.

In climates with freezing weather, vacant REO properties are usually winterized soon after they are secured. Winterization protects the plumbing and heating systems from freezing in a house where the heat is off.

A typical winterization includes shutting off the water at the main or the street, draining the supply lines and water heater, blowing out lines with compressed air, adding non-toxic antifreeze to drain traps and toilets, and, for hot water or steam heating systems, draining or protecting the boiler and radiation. A notice is usually posted at the water shutoff or main entry stating that the property has been winterized and should not have water turned on without a pressure test.

When winterization was done well and the house has stayed secure, de-winterizing and pressure-testing may show few problems. When it was done poorly, late or not at all, the damage can be extensive:
- Split copper and PEX supply lines, burst fittings and cracked shutoff valves.
- Cracked toilet tanks and bowls.
- Ruptured water heaters.
- Cracked boiler sections, burst radiators and baseboard heating loops.
- Damaged washing machine valves, ice makers and outdoor hose bibs.
- Water damage to ceilings, walls, floors and finished basements when a line burst while water was still on.

Freeze damage is often invisible until water pressure is restored. The safe approach is to restore water under controlled conditions and run a pressure test before opening fixtures, with a plumber ready to isolate failures. Estimates for winterized properties should include de-winterization, a pressure test and an explicit contingency for freeze damage.

sections.h2: Moisture, mold and roof leaks in vacant homes
sections.body:
Moisture is the second major REO problem, and it is closely linked to vacancy. A house with no heat, no air conditioning, no air circulation and no one noticing leaks can develop serious moisture damage in a single season.

Common moisture sources in REO properties include:
- Roof leaks that went unreported because no one was there to see the stain.
- Plumbing leaks from freeze damage or failed fittings.
- Groundwater and drainage problems in basements and crawlspaces, sometimes worsened by a failed sump pump with the power off.
- High humidity in closed houses in warm climates without air conditioning.
- Clogged gutters and downspouts directing water at the foundation.

The result can be mold growth on drywall, framing, subfloors, carpet and contents; rotted subfloors and framing; damaged insulation; and staining and odor that remain after the source is fixed.

A renovation plan should identify and stop the moisture source first, then assess the extent of damage, then remediate, then rebuild. Remediating mold without fixing the leak only produces new mold. Where mold is extensive, many owners and investors bring in a mold assessor or a remediation contractor following recognized industry practices before general renovation begins. Some jurisdictions have specific rules about who may perform mold assessment or remediation, so check local requirements.

In humid regions, the quickest wins after securing a vacant house are often restoring power, running dehumidification and getting air conditioning working again, which limits further growth while the scope is developed.

Vacant houses attract theft and vandalism. When you walk an REO property, assume that anything valuable and removable may be gone or damaged.

Things commonly missing from REO properties:
- Appliances: ranges, refrigerators, dishwashers, microwaves, washers and dryers. Sometimes the previous occupants took them, and sometimes they were stolen later.
- Copper: supply piping, electrical wiring pulled from walls or the service entrance, and HVAC line sets.
- HVAC equipment: outdoor condensers are frequent targets, and furnaces and water heaters are sometimes removed.
- Fixtures: light fixtures, faucets, ceiling fans, cabinet hardware and sometimes cabinets and vanities.
- Doors, garage door openers, mailboxes and house numbers.

Vandalism can include broken windows and doors, holes punched in drywall, graffiti, deliberate flooding and fire damage. Squatters may leave debris, damage, unpermitted electrical connections and pest infestations.

In an estimate, missing items should be listed individually so the owner or buyer can see exactly what must be replaced. Missing copper, in particular, can mean a partial or full repipe or rewire, and stolen wiring at the service entrance may require utility coordination before power can be restored.

Trash and contents are another common condition. Personal property left behind, food waste, debris and abandoned vehicles may require handling under rules that govern abandoned property, and servicers typically have their own procedures. Debris removal should be its own line in any REO estimate, and on some houses it is a large line.

sections.h2: Code violations, vacant building rules and permits
sections.body:
Vacant properties draw the attention of local code enforcement. Neighbors complain about tall grass, open doors, broken windows and pests, and inspectors cite the owner. By the time an REO property is ready for renovation, it may carry open violations, fines or orders.

Typical violations on vacant properties include:
- Unsecured openings, broken windows and doors.
- Overgrown lawns, weeds and accumulated trash.
- Damaged roofs, gutters, siding and fences.
- Pest and rodent infestations.
- Unsafe structures, porches, stairs and railings.
- Work done without permits by a prior owner.

Many cities and some counties have vacant building registration ordinances that require owners of vacant properties to register them, maintain insurance, post contact information and meet specific maintenance and security standards. Requirements vary widely, so the first step on any REO renovation is to check with the local building and code enforcement departments for open violations, registration status and any pending orders.

Open violations can affect closing, permit issuance and the order in which work must be done. Some jurisdictions require a pre-sale or point-of-sale inspection, and some require violations to be cleared before a new owner can occupy the property or obtain a certificate of occupancy.

Unpermitted work by a previous owner is a particular risk. Finished basements, additions, decks and electrical changes done without permits may have to be inspected, opened up, corrected or removed. An estimate that does not account for this can be badly wrong.

sections.h2: Property preservation vs renovation: what is the difference?
sections.body:
Two very different kinds of work happen on REO properties, and confusing them causes problems with scope, pricing and payment.

Property preservation is work that protects and maintains a vacant property's condition while it is held. It includes:
- Initial securing: changing locks, boarding broken openings, posting notices.
- Winterization and periodic re-winterization.
- Lawn care, snow removal and exterior maintenance.
- Debris and trash removal.
- Emergency repairs to stop further damage, such as roof tarps or water shutoffs.
- Routine inspections and condition reporting with photos.
- Pest control and removal of hazards.

Preservation is typically governed by servicer or investor guidelines that set what work may be done, how it is documented and what it may cost before additional approval is needed.

Renovation is work that changes the property's condition to prepare it for sale or rent. It includes repairs and improvements such as roofs, mechanicals, kitchens, baths, flooring and paint, and it is usually driven by a marketing decision about what the owner expects to recover.

The distinction matters because preservation and renovation are often approved, budgeted and paid through different channels, and work in one category does not automatically authorize work in the other. A preservation contractor who replaces a water heater without renovation approval may not be paid for it.

Genstone's affiliate Genstone Field Services handles property preservation, inspections and code compliance, while Genstone Construction handles the renovation side. Keeping the two clearly separated in scope and documentation is what makes an REO project easier to approve and close out.

Working for a bank, servicer, GSE or fund means working inside a documentation system. The institution needs evidence that each dollar was spent on authorized work that was actually completed, both for its own controls and for the investors, insurers and auditors it answers to.

Requirements differ by client, but commonly include:
- Bids in the client's required format, often line-itemed with quantities and unit costs.
- Photo documentation of conditions before work, sometimes for every bid line.
- Approval before work begins, with any work over a set threshold or outside routine categories requiring separate approval.
- Progress photos during work, especially of items that will be concealed.
- Completion photos taken from the same angles as the before photos.
- Invoices matching approved bid lines.
- Permits and inspection sign-offs where the work requires them.
- Lien waivers and proof of contractor insurance and licensing.
- Timely updates through the client's vendor management platform or portal.

Common reasons for rejected invoices include photos that do not clearly show the condition or the completed work, work performed before approval, items not on the approved bid and missing permits.

The practical discipline is the same on every job: photograph before you touch anything, wait for approval, photograph while concealed work is open, photograph when finished, and invoice only approved lines. A contractor who builds that routine into every crew's workflow saves the client time and gets paid faster.

sections.h2: How to estimate and plan an REO renovation
sections.body:
Estimating an REO property requires more humility than estimating an occupied house, because more of the house cannot be verified at the walkthrough.

Start by finding out the property's status. Is it winterized? Are utilities on? Are there open code violations or a vacant building registration? Was there a fire or flood claim? Is anyone occupying it? Each answer changes the plan.

Walk the exterior and the roof carefully, since roof leaks drive interior damage. Inspect the basement or crawlspace for water, mold and structural issues. Look for missing piping, wiring, equipment and fixtures. Note every sign of moisture.

If you can, get utilities restored and run a pressure test before finalizing the estimate. Systems that cannot be tested should be priced with clear assumptions and a contingency for failure.

Build the estimate in phases:
- Stabilize: debris removal, securing, moisture control, mold assessment and remediation where needed, emergency roof work.
- Restore systems: de-winterize, pressure-test, repair or replace plumbing, electrical and HVAC, address missing components.
- Correct code issues and unpermitted work.
- Renovate finishes to the level the sale or rental plan supports.
- Clean and close out with documentation.

State assumptions plainly: what was tested, what was not, and what happens if a hidden condition appears. Carry a larger contingency than you would for an occupied house of similar age.

Finally, plan the documentation from day one. On REO work, the photo record and paperwork are part of the deliverable, not an afterthought.

faqs.q: What does REO mean in real estate?
faqs.a: REO stands for real estate owned. It refers to a property owned by a lender or investor, such as a bank, servicer, GSE or fund, after a foreclosure sale failed to attract a third-party buyer or after the borrower transferred the property through a deed in lieu of foreclosure. The owner's goal is usually to sell the property, sometimes after renovation, while protecting its value in the meantime.

faqs.q: What are the most common problems in bank-owned homes?
faqs.a: The most common problems are freeze damage to plumbing and heating systems, moisture and mold from unnoticed leaks, missing appliances, copper, fixtures and HVAC equipment, vandalism and debris, deferred maintenance on roofs and exteriors, and open code violations. Most stem from long vacancy. Because systems often cannot be tested until utilities are restored, REO estimates usually carry more contingency than estimates for occupied homes.

faqs.q: How do you de-winterize a vacant house safely?
faqs.a: De-winterizing should be done by a plumber under controlled conditions. The water supply is restored gradually and the system is pressure-tested before fixtures are opened, so any split lines, cracked fittings or damaged fixtures can be found and isolated without flooding the house. Antifreeze is flushed from traps and toilets, and the water heater is refilled before power or gas is restored to it. Heating systems with water or steam need their own inspection.

faqs.q: What is the difference between property preservation and renovation?
faqs.a: Property preservation protects and maintains a vacant property while it is held: securing, winterization, lawn care, debris removal, emergency repairs and inspections. Renovation changes the property's condition to prepare it for sale or rent, through repairs and improvements to systems and finishes. They are usually approved and paid through different channels, and approval for one does not authorize work in the other.

faqs.q: Why do servicers require so many photos?
faqs.a: Servicers and institutional owners must show their investors, insurers and auditors that money was spent on authorized work that was actually completed. Before photos document the original condition and justify the bid. Progress photos show concealed work before it is covered. After photos confirm completion. Missing or unclear photos are one of the most common reasons invoices are rejected or delayed.
